title: 二楼阳台上  (Up on the Balcony)

segments.t: Bright Friday morning sunshine fills the upper courtyard balcony of Courtyard Inn. Chen taps each heavy timber post with his palm while Hao checks measurements in his leather notebook and Qing holds a basket of folded paper lanterns. Listen first.
站在二楼看出去，风景真好——整棵院子树和梧桐巷都看得见！
这整排栏杆都是风干老橡木，连一颗松动的螺丝都没有。
你看横梁上这四个铁环——正好每隔两米装一个。
这么说三十个夏天前，他们真的从这儿拉了四条金绳到院子树那儿！
志豪，你摸摸这铁环内侧，被老麻绳磨得多光滑。
要是我们往左拉两条、往右拉两条，每张桌子都能照到暖光。
志豪，最底下的灯笼挂起来，离周经理头顶有多高？
足足三米高——就算周经理高兴得跳起来，眼镜也碰不到！
说到老板，他怎么从早上八点就一直待在九号房里没出来？
他买了一大卷白海报纸，还买了一瓶蓝墨水呢！
哎呀——他不会是在给二十八位客人画正式的周年座位表吧？
小晴，记着我的话：大张海报纸碰上星期五的风，准没好事。
Now let's go through it line by line with the English translation.
站在二楼看出去，风景真好——整棵院子树和梧桐巷都看得见！

'What a view from up here—you can see the whole courtyard tree and Wutong Lane!' Qing calls the scenery "fengjing" and uses "kan de jian" ("can see") instead of plain "kan" to stress how clear the view is from the balcony.
这整排栏杆都是风干老橡木，连一颗松动的螺丝都没有。

'This entire railing is solid seasoned oak, without a single loose bolt anywhere.' Pairing "lian" ("even") with "dou meiyou" ("not have") creates the everyday pattern "not even one," while "songdong" means loose or wobbly.
你看横梁上这四个铁环——正好每隔两米装一个。

'Look at these four iron rings along the beam—spaced exactly two meters apart.' In "mei ge liang mi", "mei ge" means "at every interval of" and "liang mi" uses "liang" rather than "er" when counting two meters.
这么说三十个夏天前，他们真的从这儿拉了四条金绳到院子树那儿！

'So thirty summers ago, they really strung four golden cords from here to the courtyard tree!' Opening with "zheme" + "shuo" (literally "saying it this way") connects what Qing just learned to the past, while "la le" shows the cords were stretched across.
志豪，你摸摸这铁环内侧，被老麻绳磨得多光滑。

'Feel how smooth the inside of this iron ring is from old hemp rope, Hao.' Doubling "mo" into "momo" softens the request into "give it a quick feel," while "mo de duo guanghua" expresses "worn so smooth."
要是我们往左拉两条、往右拉两条，每张桌子都能照到暖光。

'If we angle two lines left and two lines right, every table gets warm light.' "Wang zuo" and "wang you" pair direction marker "wang" ("toward") with left and right, and "dou neng" guarantees every single table gets light.
志豪，最底下的灯笼挂起来，离周经理头顶有多高？
'How high above Zhou's head will the lowest lantern hang, Hao?' "Li" measures the distance away from Zhou's head ("touding"), and "you duo gao" is the natural way to ask "how high is it."
足足三米高——就算周经理高兴得跳起来，眼镜也碰不到！
'A full three meters high—even if Zhou jumps for joy, his glasses won't get bumped!' Repeating "zu" in "zuzu" emphasizes "a full, solid" three meters, while "peng bu dao" means "unable to bump into."
说到老板，他怎么从早上八点就一直待在九号房里没出来？

'Speaking of the boss, why has he stayed inside Room Nine since eight this morning?' "Shuodao" is a handy phrase that smoothly shifts the topic ("speaking of"), while "yizhi" shows Zhou staying put inside Room Nine all morning.
他买了一大卷白海报纸，还买了一瓶蓝墨水呢！

'He bought a huge roll of white poster paper and a bottle of blue ink!' Count flat rolled paper with "yi da juan" ("one big roll") and bottled ink with "yi ping" ("one bottle"), ending with lively "ne" for emphasis.
哎呀——他不会是在给二十八位客人画正式的周年座位表吧？

'Uh-oh—don't tell me he's drawing a formal anniversary seating chart for twenty-eight guests?' "Buhui shi ... ba" voices a playful worry ("don't tell me he's..."), and "wei" counts "ershiba" (twenty-eight) guests politely.
小晴，记着我的话：大张海报纸碰上星期五的风，准没好事。

'Mark my words, Qing: big sheets of poster paper meeting Friday wind rarely end quietly.' "Jizhe wo de hua" literally means "keep my words in mind," and "zhun mei hao shi" predicts trouble with cheeky certainty.
Now let's listen to the whole conversation one last time.

The upper balcony rings are rock solid, while downstairs in Room Nine Zhou is busy creating a giant paper masterpiece. See you next time.
回头见！
